Today I'd like to talk about one of the most remarkable skills in the animal kingdom: the camouflage of the octopus. Many animals hide by matching their surroundings, but most can do it only in one place, like a moth on tree bark. An octopus can change its appearance in less than a second, and it can do so against almost any background. Here's the interesting part: the octopus is colorblind. Its eyes contain only one type of light-sensitive cell, so scientists long wondered how it could match colors it couldn't see. One idea is that the animal's skin itself contains proteins that detect light, so the skin may be sensing the surroundings directly. Another is that the octopus uses the shape of its pupil to compare light of different wavelengths. Neither explanation has been proved. What we do know is the hardware. The skin contains thousands of tiny sacs of pigment, each controlled by muscles. When the muscles contract, the sacs stretch and the color appears. Because the system is wired directly to the nervous system, rather than relying on hormones, the change happens almost instantly.

Some Roman buildings are nearly two thousand years old and still standing. The Pantheon in Rome, for example, has the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. Modern concrete often starts to crumble after fifty or a hundred years, so engineers have long asked what the Romans did differently. A key ingredient was volcanic ash, which the Romans mixed with lime and water. The ash reacts with the lime over time and forms very stable compounds, so the material can actually become stronger. Recent studies found something else. Roman concrete contains small white chunks of lime, which scholars used to blame on sloppy mixing. In fact, the lime was added in a dry, reactive form, in a process known as hot mixing, and that produces those chunks deliberately. When a crack opens and water seeps in, the lime chunks dissolve and then harden again, filling the crack. In other words, the concrete can repair itself. Researchers are now testing similar recipes, hoping to produce modern concrete that lasts for centuries.

Today we will learn about lighthouses. A lighthouse is a tall tower with a bright light at the top. It helps ships stay safe at night. Long ago, sailors could not see the rocks near the coast in the dark, and many ships hit them. So people built lighthouses on high places near dangerous rocks. At first, workers burned wood or oil to make the light. Later, a special glass lens made the light much brighter, so ships could see it from far away. Today, most lighthouses use electricity, and ships use computers to find their way, but some lighthouses still work.

Today I'll explain how sourdough bread is made. Sourdough does not use dried yeast from a packet. Instead, a baker mixes flour and water and leaves it on the counter for several days. Tiny living things from the air and the flour, called wild yeast and bacteria, begin to grow in the mixture. They eat the flour and make a gas. The gas makes small bubbles that make the bread rise. The bacteria also make the bread taste a little sour. Bakers keep a small part of this mixture, called a starter, and use it again and again, sometimes for many years.

Until now, students could book an appointment up to a month ahead, but many reserved slots and then didn't show up, so tutors often sat idle while other students were turned away. Drop-in tutoring for short questions, such as formatting citations, will continue on weekdays between noon and one.

The ocean is often described in layers, and the main way scientists divide it is by how much sunlight reaches each layer. In the top two hundred meters, the sunlit zone, there is enough light for photosynthesis, so this is where nearly all marine plants and algae live. Below that is the twilight zone, down to about a thousand meters. A little light penetrates here, but not enough for photosynthesis. Many animals in the twilight zone make a daily journey: they rise toward the surface at night to feed, then descend at dawn. In terms of the total mass of animals involved, it is the largest migration on Earth. Below a thousand meters lies the midnight zone, where no sunlight reaches at all. Here, many creatures produce their own light, a phenomenon called bioluminescence, which they use to attract prey, to confuse predators, or to find mates. Because food is scarce in the deep, much of it consists of dead organisms sinking from above, often called marine snow.

Let's talk about mangrove forests, which grow along tropical coasts where land meets the sea. Mangrove trees face a harsh environment: their roots sit in salty water, which would kill most plants. Mangroves have solved this problem in several ways. Some species filter salt at the roots, so that very little enters the tree. Others take in salt but store it in old leaves, which later fall off, carrying the salt away. The roots themselves are remarkable. Many mangroves have tangled roots that rise above the mud, and these roots do two jobs: they supply oxygen to the tree, since mud contains little, and they slow incoming waves. That second function has practical value. Studies after major storms have found that villages behind mangrove belts often suffered less damage than those without them. Yet mangroves are disappearing, because they are cleared for shrimp farms and coastal building. Some governments are now paying communities to replant them, though newly planted forests take decades to match the protection of older ones.

tasks.title: Read an Academic Passage
tasks.text:
How Birds Find Their Way

Every autumn, billions of birds travel thousands of kilometers to warmer regions, and many return to the same small area each spring. How do they navigate? Scientists have found that birds do not rely on a single sense but combine several. During the day, many species use the position of the sun, adjusting for the time of day with an internal clock. At night, some migrants appear to read the pattern of the stars.

Birds also seem to sense Earth's magnetic field. In classic experiments, European robins kept in cages became restless at the season of migration and consistently hopped toward the direction they would fly in the wild. When researchers altered the magnetic field around the cages, the birds changed direction accordingly, even though they could not see the sky.

Still, these tools may serve different purposes. Magnetic cues provide a general heading, whereas familiar landmarks, such as coastlines and rivers, probably help birds make final corrections near their destination. Because some young birds make their first journey without guidance from adults, scientists believe that a basic sense of direction is inherited, while detailed knowledge of landmarks is learned.

How Bats Find Food

Most bats hunt at night, when it is too dark to see well. Instead of using their eyes, they use sound. A bat makes very high sounds that people cannot hear. The sounds hit insects and come back to the bat as echoes. The bat listens to the echoes and learns where the insect is, how big it is, and how fast it is moving. This way of finding things is called echolocation. Some bats can catch hundreds of small insects in one hour. Because of this, bats help farmers by eating insects that damage crops.

tasks.title: Read an Academic Passage
tasks.text:
The Thawing Ground

Permafrost, ground that remains frozen for at least two consecutive years, underlies roughly a quarter of the land in the Northern Hemisphere. For millennia it has acted as a vast freezer, locking away the remains of plants and animals that died long ago. Because the cold prevents these remains from decomposing, enormous quantities of carbon have accumulated in the frozen soil, perhaps twice as much as is currently in the atmosphere.

As the Arctic warms, however, this arrangement is becoming precarious. When permafrost thaws, microbes begin to break down the ancient material, releasing carbon dioxide and methane, a gas that traps heat far more effectively than carbon dioxide does over short periods. Scientists worry about a feedback loop: warming releases gases, which in turn cause more warming.

Thawing also threatens people directly. Much of the ground is held together by ice, so when it melts, the surface can sink or collapse, damaging roads, pipelines and buildings. Researchers caution, however, that predictions remain uncertain. Warming does not thaw all permafrost at the same rate, and in some places new vegetation may absorb part of the carbon that is released, partly offsetting the losses.

email.title: Write an Email
email.subject: Change to my volunteer shift
email.prompt:
You volunteer at your university's community garden. The coordinator, Ms. Delgado, assigned you to the Saturday morning shift for the whole month. This week you learned that your part-time job at a bookstore now requires you to work on Saturday mornings. You still want to keep volunteering.

Write an email to Ms. Delgado. In your email, do the following:
- Explain your situation.
- Suggest a different time when you could volunteer.
- Ask how she would like you to handle this Saturday's shift, which you cannot cover.

Use full sentences, and write as much as you can.
email.rubric: Task: polite email to a volunteer coordinator about a schedule conflict. Must cover all 3 bullets: (1) the situation (assigned Saturday mornings, new bookstore shift at the same time), (2) a concrete alternative time (for example Saturday afternoon or a weekday evening), (3) a clear question about this Saturday's shift (find a replacement, give notice, make up the hours). Look for an apologetic but positive tone, a statement that the writer wants to keep volunteering, greeting and sign-off, logical order, accurate grammar and precise vocabulary. Typical strong length 100-150 words.

discussion.title: Write for an Academic Discussion
discussion.prompt:
Your professor is teaching a class on economics. Post a reply to the professor's question. In your reply, do these two things.
- State your view and back it up.
- Add something new to the thread, in your own words.
Aim for at least 100 words.

professor.name: Dr. Navarro
professor.text: Several companies and a few city governments have tested a four-day workweek in which employees keep their full pay but work about 32 hours instead of 40. Supporters say workers become more focused and less stressed, so productivity does not fall. Critics say that many jobs, such as hospitals, shops and customer service, cannot simply close for a day, and that the costs may fall on other workers. Do you think a four-day workweek should become the standard? Why or why not?

students.name: Camila
students.text: I think it should. My aunt's company tried it for six months, and people were happier and made fewer mistakes. If workers are rested, they do the same work in less time, so nobody loses anything.

students.name: Owen
students.text: I'm not so sure. In my summer job at a restaurant, we needed people every day. A shorter week would mean hiring more staff or making others work longer hours, and many small businesses can't afford that.

discussion.rubric: Task: academic discussion post, 100+ words. Look for a clear position, specific support (productivity, stress, service jobs, costs for small businesses, how the change is introduced), engagement with Camila's or Owen's point that adds a new angle rather than repeating it, coherence, and varied accurate grammar and vocabulary.

interview.title: Take an Interview
interview.instructions: An interviewer will ask you four questions. There is no preparation time. You have 45 seconds to answer each question.
interview.context: You are joining a research study about how people choose where to live. A researcher will ask you some questions in a short online interview.

items.text: Thanks for taking part in this study about how people choose where to live. First, could you describe the kind of neighborhood you would most like to live in?
Some people prefer to live close to their work or school, while others are willing to travel far for a better home. Which do you prefer, and why?
Some people think that living with roommates is the best way to save money and make friends, while others value their privacy. What's your view?
Finally, some cities are encouraging people to live in smaller apartments in order to reduce housing costs. Do you think this is a good idea? Why or why not?
